facts: I started using AI for programming more than two years before the original interview.
I have AI integrated into my IDE and primarily use Gemini as a chatbot to bounce ideas around, for ideation and research.
I use Gemini to dive deeply into specific topics and investigate unfamiliar subjects. I work in a domain with deep, rich knowledge.
I use AI to understand where my industry is moving; as a software developer I also use it for debugging. I feel that virtually every aspect of my work is affected by AI.
I also use AI for what the transcript renders as 'troll through locks' (the exact activity is uncertain), and generally for just about everything in my work.
I use AI very often to write code, debug, refactor and write tests, and often to understand unfamiliar code.
I use AI often for documentation and very often for exploring concepts and learning.
My current programming task involves introducing a new capability to be used across the engineering organization where I work.
For this organization-wide capability I need to work on infrastructure in an unfamiliar part of the code base, rather than my usual application-level or pipeline work. I begin by opening my editor.

For the infrastructure task I open Claude Code with an idea of where the change might happen. I ask it to investigate the project structure, conventions and architectural decisions to give me an overview because I do not know this code base; then I describe what I want to implement.

During exploration Claude Code suggests where to put the implementation. I do not auto-accept changes: I approve or reject them and explain modifications. I may question whether this is even the right repository. I am learning to use my GitHub MCP to query the organization's repositories, locate the appropriate code and pull in more context. I use Open Spec for structured AI-assisted implementation. I said it has four commands, naming explore, propose and implement. I explore until Claude has enough context, then propose a feature specification and design. I correct the direction and design where needed; it is usually not one-shot. I review and accept an implementation plan, typically with five to ten steps and substeps. At the implementation stage of the Open Spec workflow, I either let the agent finish passively or actively approve every change, depending on the situation. I ask for a Git pull request, review its text and review the PR myself; I spend substantial time reviewing Claude-generated code.

Testing is important in my AI coding workflow. I use formatting hooks that run after changes and a claude.md file containing general agent rules and commit guidelines. In repositories whose structure I trust, I specify a test-driven workflow where each change has a test, is semantically meaningful and creates a commit. I review commits for meaningfulness and content, either during implementation or at the end, rather than working exclusively at the level of individual code changes.

While implementing or refactoring in an unfamiliar repository, I may discover additional issues, such as an unconsidered security aspect. I use an MCP server to have Claude create or update Jira tickets so the issue is captured and I can continue. I do this quite often to keep my work transparent.

In corporate development I use the context gathered in Claude or another agent not only for specifications but also to communicate work: create Jira tickets or epics describing details, or update tickets with missing information. I may ask Claude to search the internet or use an MCP server I think is called Context 7 to retrieve information about a programming language or library.
Yeah, that was a lot, but I hope.
Yeah.

I rated reviewing code as very often in my general work.
I rated bug fixing and debugging as very often in my general work; I then began to discuss running tests.
Compared with other activities I spend time on tests rarely: I have good test coverage, but tests are written quickly and I can skim them quickly, so I spend little time on the tests themselves.
In general development work I rated specification and working with requirements as often, and documentation as sometimes.
I reaffirmed documentation as sometimes and rated continuous learning as often in my general work.
Mm.
Although reviewing and debugging were rated very often, I think writing code takes the most time in my current situation.
I warned that my current working situation is unusual and may not represent the general developer population.
Mm.

I am working on a large migration project involving moving and restructuring code, so much code needs to be written. Reviewing takes almost as much time as writing, and the two are nearly inseparable because most of the code being written is not written by me.
When the question was clarified to mean code written by other team members, rather than AI, I said I work with such code sometimes, not very often.
I think I already mentioned most of my professional uses of AI because I use it for essentially everything, including debugging.
I use AI for documentation, feature development, specifications and researching ideas; I think it would be easier to ask which aspects of my work I do not use AI for.
I do not think there is any aspect of my professional work in which I do not use AI at all.
Yeah.
I used to complete comparable programming tasks without AI, but no longer do so.
Compared with working without AI, I spend much less time testing, writing and thinking about tests, and fiddling with unfamiliar code or libraries. I can spend more time on architecture.
With AI-assisted development I spend less time worrying about very specific aspects of the code.
My AI-assisted work focuses more on imposing structure. I compare my role to an orchestra conductor: someone can program for me under my direction, and I can micromanage when required.

I think AI makes me able to write more code and be more effective in outcomes; some tasks finish quickly, allowing more time to think about problems rather than implementation. The downside is losing some connection with and deep understanding of the code: even when I think I understand my conceptual model, I may later discover a function I have not seen before, unlike when writing manually.

I am thinking about harnesses to assure AI-generated code quality: observability, testing, monitoring and qualitative or quantitative measures such as speed. I write pipelines with industry-specific knowledge and must know they produce correct outputs and perform optimally. I think a data-driven approach that establishes correctness and efficiency would make AI powerful for tasks that used to take much of my time.

With AI I feel less locked in and less involved with my tools; I experience flow less, or perhaps differently. I used to enjoy and optimize efficient IDE navigation and personal workflows, but spend less time on that now. I feel I have lost some of that involvement in exchange for productivity.

To decide whether to rely on AI, in a new repository I first read and understand the concepts and surrounding structure. Later I can allow more autonomy if I have rules and a harness defining permissible actions. I see unconstrained vibe coding as dangerous: a direct request to build an app or feature may produce a tactically correct result with minimal effort but fail to follow architectural patterns and accumulate technical debt. I still consider myself a bottleneck because I have to review everything the AI does.

I think AI-driven development is changing extremely fast. At the original interview I believed Claude Code was no more than about a year old and the best tool then for AI-driven software development, but I could not predict what came next. I recalled ChatGPT appearing in 2022, followed by a period of asking it questions and copy-pasting code before integration into development tools. I worry research and experiments may lose relevance within a month because the field changes so fast.
I characterized my comments about rapid AI change and research relevance as a high-level thought.

I think current AI can reason at high levels but lacks a form of knowledge compaction: in my experience humans abstract patterns in sleep, from words to structures and concepts, while AI is poor at holistic understanding and still needs my guidance. entries.topic: 模型幻觉与无监督学习
entries.text: 模型幻觉与无监督学习应作概念区分：模型幻觉是模型输出缺少可靠依据或包含错误断言的现象；无监督学习是从无标签数据中发现结构或模式。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
监督学习与强化学习应作概念区分：监督学习是用带标签样本拟合输入到输出的映射；强化学习是通过环境反馈和奖励优化行动策略。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
强化学习与训练集应作概念区分：强化学习是通过环境反馈和奖励优化行动策略；训练集是用于拟合模型参数的数据样本。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
过拟合与精确率应作概念区分：过拟合是模型学习了训练样本特有噪声而难以泛化；精确率是预测为正的样本中实际为正的比例。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
过拟合（overfitting）：模型学习了训练样本特有噪声而难以泛化。
欠拟合与大语言模型应作概念区分：欠拟合是模型表达能力或训练程度不足导致规律学习不充分；大语言模型是从大规模文本等序列学习条件生成分布的模型。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
验证集（validation set）：用于选择超参数和比较方案的数据。

过拟合与召回率应作概念区分：过拟合是模型学习了训练样本特有噪声而难以泛化；召回率是实际为正的样本中被正确识别的比例。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
